utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Could we have the appearances now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, along with Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can I have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Tomislav Kuzmanovic on behalf of Mr. Mucic. I would make a request of the Court. My client, at 2.00, has a mass at the prison, and he has granted me the authority to state that should the trial go beyond into this afternoon, that he has given permission for the trial to continue from his perspective without his presence. So I would ask that -- make that request that he be allowed to attend mass at 2.00 this afternoon. It's his name's day mass, and the priest is going to be in the prison for this mass and that's the basis for the request. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence Counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. Mr. Hazim Delic is also represented by my colleague, Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Cynthia McMurrey, and along with my co-counsel, Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my client, Mr. Zejnil Delalic, has some health problems, has had them for several days, and today his situation worsened. He's being examined. I have contacted with him and he has given me authorisation to tell you that the trial can go on without his presence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think Mr. Mucic might be able to attend his mass at the appointed time, as long as you continue to represent his interest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the witness now. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Inform the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Demic, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, you can proceed with your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Demic.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you rest a little bit? I know it was a long journey.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I slept a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, let's go back to the part of the conversation where we left off, when our time expired yesterday. Beforehand, Mr. Demic, in order to clarify completely what you were saying yesterday before this Tribunal, can you tell us one more time where did you go after you taped the interview at the Celebici barracks, and how it happened that you met with Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I believe that there was nothing unclear there. When -- I think that I can even recollect every curve of the road between Celebici and Konjic. I can draw it for you. I know this road extremely well. We left the compound, we turned to the right towards Konjic, and behind us we left a tunnel, and then there was an underpass, the railroad, and then we went along the Neretva River for about 10 kilometres, until we reached the first houses. And the first house is the house of Mr. Delalic. All other houses are across the river. So we are going along the river and there are villages along there. And on the other side there is a hill and the forest, and then there are up there, there are some houses and some clearings. Then you enter Konjic. On the one side is the gas station. At the other side is a tire repair shop and the car wash. And then we arrived at Mr. Delalic's house. He stepped out of his house. The gas station was closed. He waved to us and made a signal to stop. We were driving in a car, a Wartburg, which is an East German car make.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, did I understand you correctly. Did you -- you did not go to see Mr. Delalic, but when you passed, when Mr. Delalic saw your vehicle, he signalled you to stop; is that -- is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: You may not have remembered, but we were very tight with time. We were going to take the material to the tower up on Mount Bjelasnica, and we were in a great hurry. So we wanted to ask someone, because in our footage we had all the stories that we needed to have, everybody who was concerned there. So we were just trying to verify the information, and not some kind of a general condition in the -- in this prison. In other words, I am not sure what you are not clear about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to that, I am going to ask you just one further question. Since you pinpointed a time when this was happening, and yesterday we saw from the interview, from the videotape, that the doctor said that two, three weeks before that he was a prisoner too. So based on all of that, the Tribunal can gain an idea about the time frame in which you made this interview. So, as you are saying, this is August, either mid-August or around 10th of August, is it true that about 10 days earlier you had met with Mr. Delalic as commander of Tactical Group at his headquarters in Pasaric?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you and your colleague, Jadranka Milosevic, know Mr. Delalic from that time on, and did he know you?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Because he was commander of this area, or of these units which were getting prepared to help in the lift of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, I believe that now the situation is much clearer, because, obviously, maybe it was the way I asked the question, but thank you for clarifying this. And I apologise for taking you back to it. The last thing I had asked you yesterday, during our conversation, was whether in this area where Mr. Delalic was in charge, was a commander of Tactical Group 1 on the tasks of lifting the siege of Sarajevo, did you then, together with your colleague, Jadranka Milosevic, receive from him an interview?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this was at Ormanje. And, yes, we did. This is an area that is in the area of Hadzici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Confine your answer to what is being asked. You are giving details in which we are not interested. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Sorry, it's a professional thing. I think we are probably paid by word, but I will take that into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think we are all clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I will please ask you, as we have been advised by the Tribunal, please try to be as succinct as possible.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: See, also, there were some unclear points, so I was just trying to be helpful and clarify it. However, I can also answer by "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would now request that excerpt number 2 be shown. It's an interview with Mr. Delalic and it's part of the evidence which has already been submitted to the Tribunal, and I believe it's part of the Exhibit No. 116 of the Prosecution. So, please, can we run excerpt number 2, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The situation in our units is very good. There are units from about 10 municipalities under my command, and include BiH armed forces and the HOS units. The HVO does not participate in this action. Moreover, they have been obstructing these operations in the Kiseljak area, the HVO units sit together in the same tent with the Chetniks. And during the capture of Ostrik, they even let the Chetnik tanks, two tanks, pass through their territory. And we informed the Supreme Command about this. In the action of the encircling of this area we will take measures regardless of what party might be involved, whether it is the HVO or the Chetniks. Considering the other aspects of the situation, our forces are several times as strong as the Chetnik ones. We are just waiting for the Supreme Command to order full attack. The Supreme Command wants to spare as many private and public buildings and to have as few civilian victims, regardless of their ethnic background. We also would like to say to the people of Sarajevo, who have been under siege and attacks for many months, that we hope to see them very soon. All our soldiers are highly motivated and we can hardly wait to hug the people from Sarajevo at Bascarsija or Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, do you recognise the persons in this videotape, in this interview?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who are these persons?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: It is Zejnil Delalic and my colleague Jadranka Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who taped this?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, you told us, previously, that this was at Ormanje. Is this a very rugged and inaccessible mountain area which was part of the effort to lift the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, this was a very rugged, very forested area, and you could only use horseback to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is it all relevant? We know he was a TG-1 commander. He was a TG-1 commander. He was engaged in fighting. So how is it all relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to ask some questions regarding this excerpt, and from them you will see that there is connection here with Mr. Delalic. Let me pose you a question right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, is it true that as early as that time there were attacks of the HVO against the army units and response of Mr. -- very decisive response of Mr. Delalic regarding that?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, it was already at that time we had tensions, especially in the area of Kiseljak, and the other commander in that area responded to that even more decisively than Mr. Delalic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, did you, as a journalist, know that as early as that period there was a propaganda campaign waged against Zejnil Delalic at that time?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. From Mostar came an attack -- I believe that this was counterintelligence attack, that he was a part of this counterintelligence group of the -- and that he was poisoning the relations between Croats and Muslims in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there will be several more questions in this area, since this is where the campaign against Mr. Delalic started. I believe that this interview is relevant and this witness recognised this interview as his own, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Microphone not on) -- that there was a campaign against him. And so what? There was a malicious campaign against Delalic, so what? What has that to do? Is it sure that he was not a commander --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not receiving your interpretation of what you are saying. Part of the evidence that the Prosecution has offered as part of the propaganda campaign here, and we have a witness who, by interviewing these relevant persons, has found out the facts, even while Mr. Delalic was on the ground in the area. And I believe that it is important that you know the facts that this witness is referring to. And this is why this witness has been called to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You say there was propaganda against him? Are you denying that there was any propaganda? Whether other propaganda was true or not, does it affect whatever was charged?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I might also add something. As I understood Ms. Residovic, this videotape is also in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 116, so there is no need to get it into evidence a second time, if it's just a portion of the same exhibit which has been admitted. Obviously, Defence Counsel can use whatever she thinks is relevant of the seized videos, just as the Prosecution can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for clarifying this, and we have just heard the witness who has authenticated this piece of evidence, and we see that this propaganda has to be countered by facts which would serve to lay the ground for the counter-propaganda that we are trying to introduce here. But, as my colleague has just said, this has already been admitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on) -- round about way. Ask him straight away about the propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: -- but he's in a position to dispute the propaganda. He's not the one, only one let it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why go the roundabout way? Straight away ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, we saw the tape, we heard the suggestions of the Trial Chamber. I already asked you this, did you know that there was -- propaganda campaign was waged against Mr. Delalic at that time, and that he was branded as a person who was betraying certain interests?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, but General Jovo Divjak was part of that package, so-to-speak, because these accusations were levelled against him as well. They were both accused of working for the same agency, that is the intelligence agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on) -- agency of?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Of the JNA or the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Demic, you know that both Mr. Delalic and Mr. Jovo Divjak were victims of this propaganda which was vociferously waged against them, even while Mr. Delalic was still in that area?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. In an interview Mr. Divjak publicly complained about it, and I believe that this was broadcast, it was a part of an interview which I made with Mr. Delalic and Mr. Fehbija Karic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So on another later occasion you taped an interview with -- an interview with Mr. Delalic, Mr. Fehbija Karic and Mr. Jovo Divjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this an interview when you asked him of their opinion as -- following the attack of the HVO in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. We attempted to enter Prozor, but we were turned back at the barrack -- at the barricade, and so we had to come back. And then we taped the interview with all three persons which you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just mentioned it, can you recall, was this -- when was this? Could this have been late October, early November?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. It was at that time we were -- later, about three or four days later, we entered Prozor and were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, is this the interview when Mr. Divjak personally pointed out the propaganda of the HVO against himself and Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Not just the HVO. I believe that there was certain circles on the Bosnian side which were either linked to the circles in the HVO or maybe for some other reasons, may be career reason. I am not going to speculate on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday, Mr. Demic, you said that as a war correspondent in the area of Mount Igman you had a number of meetings with our refugees and you conducted a number of interviews with these persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. We were the first to tape some footage from Mount Igman, and they went -- they were shown around the world through the Eurovision exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that through this you became a witness of many horrible stories of people who were fleeing the Chetnik territory?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: This was something I was listening to throughout the war, but not just listened to, but also watched.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, tell me, if there were someone from the Bosnia side, if somebody were to accuse a Bosniak of being a collaborator of the KOS the counter intelligence or of the Chetniks, what would that mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object to continued questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's an opinion. It's an opinion. --- (Kindly be advised microphone is not activated)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you're accused of being a friend of your enemy, you don't think well of him, maybe you do some violence to him. Proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, the witness can express his opinion. I am not asking a general opinion, I am asking his own opinion. I believe that everybody is very clear as to what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I believe that, in general, if somebody is accused of such a thing, he has nothing to do there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since you were in touch with thousands of such people, can you tell us where these refugees were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: More than 20.s000 civilians, elderly, women and children, came from Mount Igman in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat the same questions all over again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, when Mr. Delalic left Konjic at the end of 1992, are you a witness of even greater propaganda against Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, it was present, constantly. There was also propaganda against Mr. Mucic. Even, it was said that Mr. Delalic left the country via a helicopter of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, these few questions which were repeated were important because the Prosecutor showed the Exhibit No. 116 as a true exhibit and I have no more questions for the witness and I thank you for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the tape on the war on BH. We heard the witnesses, Cecez and in about there, there is another part of the counter propaganda material. And when you will be evaluating it, I think that the witnesses and that their testimony will be of use to you to evaluate the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are doing more than cross examination, so I suppose you are trying to fill up the gap. You could have done if he came in -- this witness came in as your witness. That is why I did not bother with the trend of your cross-examination. So if you have cross-examined sufficiently, you can then stop, but if you have not, and you still think you can use the witness in the way you could have if he was called by you, you can conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for that. But in order to clarify the situation as it was, I would like to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, is it true that I asked you to testify in this case and that you have accepted to come as a witness?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, I would have come if anybody had invited me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true, Mr. Demic, that from the 20th of May to the 19th of June, you were on a study tour in the United States and at the time you were not in a position to attend the Court hearing and to present yourself here?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The footage that you have offered to me, and particularly your original material is in your original cassette, it is totally credible material?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: It is at home, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demic. Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me this opportunity for examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I point out a point in the transcript on page 16, line 6, the transcript reads "Cecez" and I believe my colleague, Ms. Residovic, said Ciso, C-I-S-O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's hear your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to be asking you a series of questions and if they call for a yes or no answer, I would like you to just give a yes or no response, is that understood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you'd mentioned that you came upon Celebici, somewhat as a surprise; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you came upon Celebici, can you describe for the Court how far off the main road the entrance to the Celebici barracks is?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Aerially, it's not a 100 metres. But if you go by road, it's 250, 300 metres. There is a curve and a cross-roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it's right next to the, basically right next to the main road, correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the location of the camp is fairly close to the main road, 300 metres, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Couldn't be that close --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had never met Mr. Mucic prior to your coming to Celebici, correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: The answer is never before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend speaking with Mr. Mucic when you were at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Four or five minutes. Because he then went to the building, the premise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: We also said goodbye to each other when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything specific that you spoke with Mr. Mucic about other than generalities?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Generalities and we were joking. Mr. Mucic was joking. I liked it because I had a feeling that I would be able to do my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So at least as far as you were concerned, you had free access to anywhere you wanted to go? I didn't get the translation on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This question is asked yesterday by mister -- --- (Kindly be advised microphone is not activated)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Counsel for Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think his answer hasn't been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have the answer to the question. Now repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So at least as far as you're concerned, you had free access to anywhere you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not getting the Bosnian interpretation. Now I am getting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What time of day was it, sir, when you were at the camp? Now, I'm sorry, Your Honours, I am not getting any of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the English booth be heard? Yes. We have one microphone dead here in the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We still have one answer missing. The answer to the time of the day he was at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll re-ask the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was at noon. It was very hot, but I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle you were driving had a sign that was marked "Press" on it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, with yellow letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it in the windshield or was it on top of the car, could you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: On the forepart and on the windshield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it would be obvious to anyone who you were driving by or who would see your vehicle that you were a member of the press?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, and on the back there was also, instead of a licence plate -- instead of a licence plate, we had a "Press" sign on the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The clothing that was worn by your -- by the person who did the interviewing, Ms. Jadranka, correct, she had a camouflage shirt on?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, this was a gift from the General Major Divjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether she had a camouflage shirt on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he had nothing else to put on since she was a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's fairly common for even members of the press to wear camouflage shirts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually his answer would have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not common, but it was of necessity. It was not common, but it was of necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How, in terms of the -- I withdraw that question. Could you describe for us on the model, the number of people that you saw when you were in Celebici and where they were, other than the people in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I believe that I encountered some, approximately 20 people, in groups of two or three or four, often. Mixed groups between guards and prisoners. They were watering the lawn, the trees with hoses. There was a puddle in front of the administrative building. There was -- I remember these puddles because the road was uneven with holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could take the pointer that's next to you, please, and just point out -- you've pointed with your finger to the model, but if you could just point out, generally, the area with the pointer, for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Here I talked to the brother, Zara's brother. Here we have the puddles. Here a man was washing an old car, Fiat feature. Here they had water hoses. Zara's brother was there. And then Zara came from that direction. And then under the awning here, people were sitting and I didn't move further into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have a few brief questions, if I might?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, we met only met yesterday for the first time after court in the Defence witness room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, that's when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And by the way, I am Cynthia McMurrey, I represent Esad Landzo. For clarification on the camp at Celebici, I would like to ask you to stand up and use the pointer again because I don't know that it's clear. This -- can you point to where the entrance to Celebici is, to the camp? And that is the entrance that you're talking about was 250 to 300 metres away from the main road, right?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Here we have the curve and then the main road. But in aerial distance would be less. The tunnel there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, that road that goes into Celebici goes around this side of the camp and ends on M-17 at that end, doesn't it? M-17, the road between Konjic and Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, M-7 (sic), Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that main highway runs parallel to the end of the Celebici camp; is that correct? In fact, part of that road runs along that end of the camp going that way to Jablanica and that way to Konjic; would that be accurate? So this end of the camp is 250 to 300 metres from the main road, but that end of the camp is directly on the main road, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is why I said the aerial distance would be less. Precisely for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted the Court to be clear that the camp itself is actually on the main road, part of it, just not the entrance. And, also, I would like to play --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: That was not a camp, these were barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're absolutely right, the Celebici barracks. In fact, when you're standing at that end of the camp, you're looking onto the road to Mostar and another tunnel that goes on to Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You do have to answer "yes". Thank you. So that these --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At this point, Your Honour, I would like to play an excerpt of a tape and ask Mr. Demic if he can recognise it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. At approximately two minutes before ten, Mrs. McMurrey gave me copies of the transcript regarding the videotape she wants to show. And they're all interviews with, it appears, refugees, about various things that happened. They have nothing to do with Konjic and they have nothing to do with Celebici. They're just people talking about horrible things that happened to them in the war. Then I would object as to the relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may respond? At this point, as Madam Residovic also, to preclude the necessity of recalling this witness at another time. I am not asking to introduce these tapes into evidence at this point. I only would like for Mr. Demic to authenticate them. He made these tapes. He is the videographer. And at the time that the Defence puts on its case, I will show the relevance of these tapes at that point. And to prevent him from having to return, all I want to do is authenticate the tapes and I will attempt to offer them into evidence once the relevancy has been determined. But contrary to what Ms. McHenry said, these were tapes made in Konjic, in the Konjic municipality, in April, May, June of 1992. And for the Defence of Mr. Landzo, the state of mind of Mr. Landzo, and the people in the Konjic area is relevant to the Defence of diminished mental capacity. I am not going to try to introduce them into evidence at this time. I merely want to try to authenticate them through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, his evidence is related to his experience and the tapes he made in respect of Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This evidence are tapes that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you let me finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, is this tape part of that exercise of his interviews with persons in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's interviews of people in the Konjic municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because I don't see the relevancy to it in what he has made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance will be established in the defence of diminished mental capacity. It goes to the state of mind of Mr. Landzo at the time of April, May, June of 1992. What the people of Konjic were told and why they were so petrified and panicked and afraid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it is relevant to his evidence and even the defence of diminished responsibility. That is always evidence based on medical evidence. And, you know, I think it will not be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any other questions to ask, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I only want him to authenticate and reserve a ruling on relevance until after the Defence has put his case on. But if the Court wants me to authenticate it at another time, once the relevance has been determined, then I'll be happy to attempt to call him back at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Only introduce the evidence of mental, whichever way you want to talk about is his disability. We'll determine whether such a thing is relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. You're probably taking the plea of provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not provocation. It goes to his state of mind, his mental capacity at the time. This is relevant. These videos were April, May, June of 1992. What people had told him, what he was experiencing in the Konjic area in 1992. I feel that -- of course, I can't establish the relevance at this point, I merely wanted to authenticate that this man produced them. That they're accurate reconstructions of the evidence that he saw and he produced in 1992. I don't have to have an interpretation of them. I merely wanted to authenticate them at this point and reserve evidence until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My advice to you, please, is to study properly the scope, the basis of diminished responsibility. It will later arise from mental disease or defects or congenital defects developing from arrested or retarded development. So I do not see how any of these things could have arisen from whatever propaganda which was dished out at that time. So, I have not heard your arguments. When you bring up your argument with respect to the time of facts you rely for your retarded, arrested developments of mental disease, we will consider it. These are the only basis of diminished responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, since I didn't have a definition to go from, I am assuming that the definition that the Court just gave me is the one that I am working from at this point, which would be the Homicide Act of 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Court has so many psychoanalytical publications on this type of defect. You can read them widely. If you've already pleaded the Defence, and you read them, and make your submissions to the Trial Chamber in accordance with the known accepted basis of diminished responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And it also says in the parenthesis in that, that an abnormality of the mind from any cause --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Arising from mental disease or retarded, arrested development.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Right. And it's our submission to this Court that the irritation of the mental disease by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are not arguing that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am not. I was only asking to authenticate the case, but if the Court will not let me authenticate them, then I have no recourse but I pass the witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. McHenry, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, I am going to be asking you some questions. If you don't understand a question, please just indicate that and I will repeat or rephrase it. I would also just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I also remind you that you will not be paid by the number of words you use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And in that regard, sir, I will try to make a number of my questions "yes" or "no" questions for you. Sir, was there a prison in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And what would you call that where the prisoners were kept, that part of the barracks? You said it wasn't a camp, just what was it where the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I must tell you that when concerning Bosnia, you cannot rely on encyclopaedias. I was a witness when the aggression on Bosnia started. The first prisoners, that is the armed Serb rebels, were being kept in schools where the soldiers of the armed forces were also sleeping. They were looking for places where they were not -- where they would not be together. And I know for certain when somebody would say, oh, let's put them over there because that would be good. It would be a convenient place. And this was a barracks. This would be ideal conditions, you know. It was fenced off. And then also it was made to regulation by the former JNA and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, it wasn't -- you couldn't call it a prison and you couldn't call it a camp; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I am not competent to say that. I am just a journalist. To, you know, give it any designation that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree that there were prisoners there, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the interview, that you had with Mr. Delalic about Celebici, did Mrs. Milosevic, your colleague, did she know Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, I met him at a social club. I was talking to my friends and he walked by. We talked and also I saw him later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did your colleague know Mr. Delalic? Did she know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not until then. Not until the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's your testimony that the very first time that Mrs. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No, I got the interpretation whether I had known him. That is what I reserved as interpretation, so I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So according to your knowledge, the first time that Mrs. Milosevic met Mr. Delalic was with you during the interview about Celebici? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I don't know that. She also went without me. There were times when she travelled on her -- I don't know why this is important, but I cannot confirm that. I cannot say when, because when I first met him I was by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you don't know the answer to a question, all you have to do is say, "I don't know." You don't have to explain.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when was your report on Celebici broadcast on Sarajevo TV?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: That same -- the evening of the day when we first taped it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated in direct that the interview with Mr. Delalic about Celebici occurred before the swearing in at Celebici. Are you sure that the interview about Celebici was before the swearing in that occurred in Celebici, or could have been after?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if Mrs. Milosevic has reported that she believed the visit occurred on the 20th or 21st of August, would that be possible, or would that be impossible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's impeaching this witness with the statement of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm asking him a question about a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there was an effort to correct the date in his answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. I believe earlier it was brought out that he had earlier given a different date, and now I am asking whether or not it's possible that it could have occurred on the 20th or 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question in an exact way. Jadranka could have made a mistake or I could have made a mistake, but the videotape is authentic and the date is printed there. So that is not a lie, the date there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where exactly is the date imprinted? When you see the video, is the date imprinted on the video that you see?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: The date could see -- if the camera has imprinted it, it's in the lower right corner, but it's -- because it was put in the archive when it was first broadcast, so it would have borne the date when it was broadcast on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if the video doesn't have a date on it itself, the only thing you could look at is the archives to see when it was broadcast; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: It can also be verified on the cassette which had an accompanying sheet of paper, which had given the times and which my colleague, Jadranka, made. Also, our colleague, Zekira, who was a secretary probably, put together that list. Yes, her name is Zekira Topalovic. So that can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me now that your earlier testimony that the date was imprinted on the videotape was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He doesn't say that. He said he can verify it from other sources also.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, but I am trying to find out if the most direct source, if it's on the tape or not. And he initially said it was. If I understood him correctly now, he says it's not on the tape, and I am just trying to verify which of those two things is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you said it is not on the tape?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you had heard about Celebici from Pale Radio. Were you in a position to hear Pale Radio because of your profession or special occasion, or could any person in Konjic with a radio hear the Pale broadcast?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: From time to time, I also listened to Pale. I listened to other stations as well, of course, when I was in a position to do so. That is normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The exact question was, were radio broadcasts from Pale available in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, they were available. And I believe that they could be heard quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, did you hear any reports on -- about the Musala prison in Konjic on Pale Radio or just about Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I heard of Celebici and, as far as Musala is concerned, I believe I did not. I don't recall, but I did know about Musala as well, that a number of prisoners were there. As I said before, it was -- they were kept in schools, sports halls, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just remind you that often I think your explanation is just going to delay things. So if you can answer my question simply, that's all you have to do. Now, you indicated that --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: My desire is only to be more clear, so that we avoid any misunderstandings. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you said that the Serb public radio broadcast false propaganda. Was it only the Serb side that broadcast false propaganda, or did all sides, the Serb, the Croat, and the Muslim, publicise false propaganda?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I can only guarantee for my own work, but in a different degree there were -- there was propaganda. The question is only of degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, before you went to Celebici, you had talked with Mr. Delalic about your desire to visit Celebici, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This question has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I have already answered this question, and I believe that this was linked to my desire to visit Celebici, to verify the information. There was no insisting on it, just my desire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, then, you agree with me that prior to visiting Celebici you had talked to Mr. Delalic about your desire to visit the camp, the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you the way you put the question. If you can rephrase the question. There are parts where I can say "yes," and there are parts of it where I would say "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You, before the time you went to Celebici, you and Mr. Delalic had a conversation in which you indicated that you wanted to go visit Celebici; is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the position? What is the correct position?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: The correct position is that it is possible that it was -- that Mr. Delalic was there when I was talking in a circle of friends and acquaintances that I would like to visit the prison, but I do not exclude the possibility that he was present there. I don't know that he was not there. So he may have heard it also. So that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection, sir. Did you previously state, "Some days after the fall of Bradina I met Zejnil Delalic for the first time. Since I had heard the stories of the food supply in Konjic, I told Mr. Delalic about what I had heard, to see his reaction." And you are here referring to the problems of food in Celebici. "I mentioned to him that I wanted to go to the barracks to find out what was going on. He was in favour of it." Do you remember saying that in your prior statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: There are some elements there which I had mentioned here before. I recollect, absolutely, a statement of his, and it's vividly in my mind. I told him that the fighters were complaining as to why the prisoners were given more than they were, and he was accused as a logistics person who was in charge of supplying the food. And he said, "We must not be like they are. So that we should be better than them. We have to be better than them. We cannot be like Serbs or Chetniks." I don't know exactly what he said, but I absolutely recall him making that statement. That is something that has stayed in my mind as something characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So you certainly agree that you had a conversation with Mr. Delalic about the food problems in Celebici before you went there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And do you then remember going -- also stating, "I mentioned to him that I wanted to go to the barracks to find out what was going on. He was in favour of it." Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me just a second. It would be a little fairer to the witness to provide him with a copy of this statement. I have one somewhere around here in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's fine. I have a number of copies that I am happy now to provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would it help you to look at your prior statement?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Absolutely. Of course. Why not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, in fact, while that statement is being marked, sir, let me ask you: You mentioned yesterday the interview with Ms. Manke of the Office of the Prosecutor, and said you weren't really prepared for it. You would agree with me that at the time you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you had already been interviewed and given a statement to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, and it was a very short statement. And I was not straining myself in any way. Just as I have not strained myself when I came here. I didn't even bother with the videotapes. I can describe every person there, but may not remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me go on, sir. Before you look at your statement, I'll point out to you and ask you just a few other questions about that. Now, the interview with Ms. Manke was scheduled in advance, wasn't it? I mean, there was an appointment in advance and you then went to the offices of the Tribunal in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And the interview, in fact, took place over two days, on both the 19th and the 22nd of October, 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, we talked for two days. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And at the time of the interview you knew that there were ongoing procedures before the Tribunal, and indeed you knew that some persons had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that you understood that it was important for the information you gave in your signed statement to be truthful and accurate, to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes. However, I did not have the time to refresh my memory or do anything. But if you want me to tell you, we talked more about the beginning of the aggression, about Prijedor, about the statement of Karic in the assembly and things in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And at the end of the interview, the statement was read out to you and you signed it as being true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, in fact, the document that you've been shown, does it show your signature on it? Does the witness have both the English and the Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, it does have it, but I don't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the English version, sir. It's on page 6 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: This on the front page is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And on page 6 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Page 6 of the English version. Just a moment. No. Oh, yes, up there. Yes. Yes, it is. I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And I want to go -- I can only tell you in the English -- on the English version it's on page 2, the first full page of text, and there's a paragraph that starts off, "Some days after the fall of Bradina --"

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: My English is not very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If you could look at the Serbo-Croatian version and find -- or maybe Ms. Residovic is going to help us. The paragraph that begins -- it's the fourth paragraph in your statement and it starts off, "Some days after the fall of Bradina I met Zejnil Delalic for the first time --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be helpful. I think it's the last paragraph on the first page of the Bosnian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The last sentence is very meaningful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I want to direct you to the last sentence, sir. Did you say, "I mentioned to him that I wanted to go to the barracks to find out what was going on. He was in favour of it and said that he hoped that 'we,' being from state TV, would be allowed to enter the barracks." Is that what you said in your prior statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Not in this form. But there are some elements here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just ask you, sir, does this remind you --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: It also says here -- yes, it is true that this was in front of the cultural hall that we saw each other, because, you know that your colleague, Sabine, she can rephrase the sentence and she would dictate it to the person who is taking down the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is one thing I want to find out. Delalic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Delalic's reply is that he hoped that he, being from the state TV, would be allowed. If he is himself, the commander --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly would ask the witness any questions about that, but because the witness doesn't remember ever making that, I don't see how I am going to ask him any questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it still the case, sir, you don't remember whether or not you and Mr. Delalic specifically discussed the fact you wished to visit Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I don't recall every detail. And I said the way I said it. But this could be a provocation, just like in the movie. It's a kind of a likeable provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just go on. Now, you would agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me clear something. Did you ask Delalic for permission to go into the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No. Expressly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that you stated yesterday that you didn't ask anyone permission to go to Celebici, until you got -- until you actually got to the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, do you recollect, and I have copies of it, if you -- if you wish, saying to a representative of the Defence that although -- excuse me. Let me just find this. "I do not remember who we talked to about permission, but I know it was --" you are talking about the problems about what you heard about the food. "This made us go to Celebici to find out and publicise the truth. I do not remember who we talked to about permission, but I know that it was granted for the visit and the filming." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: In other words, we received the permission when -- if we showed up at the prison, or the barracks, however you decide to call it. So when I answered the question a moment ago, I was talking to a number of people there, and you need to know that it is very difficult to say -- it was very difficult there to say who was in charge, because everybody was vain, and if you were to say that somebody was subordinate to someone else, that would have been very hard. You know, this is not a textbook. This was just circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me move forward, sir. You described seeing, when you arrived at Celebici, a young guard and then Mr. Delic. It's correct, isn't it, that because of the interaction you saw between the young guard and Mr. Delic --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: A senior guard, and then I knew that it was Mr. Delic later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's correct, because of the interaction you saw between this young guard and the person you identified in court here today, you assumed that Mr. Delic was a young man superior, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I could assume, but, you know, what importance I placed to that as a journalist, none. It didn't matter at all from -- as far as my entering the camp is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you answered the question as "yes"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I could not answer that question for sure. As an assumption, yes, but not as certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you indicated where you filmed. If Jadranka Milosevic reported that Pavo indicated you could film the infirmary and that the prisoners would be brought to you, and you would not be permitted to film wherever you wanted, would that be consistent or inconsistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: We could film whatever we wanted to, and this is what we did. We filmed the infirmary too. If there was -- if it had been forbidden, I don't know how I could have filmed the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. I think there may have been a slight translation error there, but I don't think it's important enough. Let me move forward. Sir, were you aware that prisoners were kept in a tunnel in Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And besides the infirmary, did you make any request to view the areas where the prisoners were kept, besides the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No, we did not. We saw a lot of them outside, and we heard the one who was the most prominent among them, we heard the ones who distributed food, we heard the doctors, and we talked to those who were injured, who were in the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that, and I am not going to be asking you here, with rare exception, to repeat what you said yesterday. So if the answer is a simple no, you don't have to explain it by repeating what you've already said. Now, at any time when you were in Celebici, did you see Pavo with a video camera of his own?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how about when you were at the swearing in, did you see Mr. Mucic at that time?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I did see Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Because he spoke to those assembled. I really don't recall about Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, the time that you were in Celebici about the prisoners, you indicated that Mucic came in and out of the administration building. Did you ever go in the administration building to say good-bye or for any reason?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No. The door was wide open. We greeted each other outside and we said good-bye to each other outside. We thanked them and we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So let me just clarify. When you indicated that it was too warm to sit inside the administration building, that was just an assumption you made because of the heat, not because you yourself felt how warm it was inside there?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, that's an assumption. I saw that the door was opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, before your interview with the doctors in the barracks, did anyone have the opportunity to talk with them about the subject of their testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to object to the form of the question, saying that what the doctor said was testimony. I don't believe that what the doctor said was testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'd say there was an interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you correcting the interpretation or the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question, as interpreted, perhaps, stated that what the doctor said on the videotape was testimony, and my question was to the form of the question. If it was an interpretation problem, then we'll have to deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It couldn't be an interpretation problem from English to English. I mean, we don't do that too. The word she used was "testimony".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was no confusion in your question. There is none. Can you give an answer, whether you saw anyone who was being questioned?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No, no one. Really, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, I think the Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Tell the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, may I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, immediately before the break, you indicated that no one had the opportunity to talk with the doctors about the subject of their interview before you started talking to them. So is it correct that if both the doctors and Mr. Delalic have said that before the filming of your interview, Mr. Delalic talked to the doctors about their interview, they would all be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Incorrect. At least as far as I know that is incorrect. And on that day, it was just we who talked to the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And it was just by chance that you decided to stop by. So if I understand you correctly, according to your testimony, it wouldn't have been possible for anyone to talk to the doctors beforehand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How can he say that? What might have been possible? How can he say that? It would not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, if he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that you stopped by just by chance?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Absolutely. In Ostrozac, we decided to try our luck. I don't see why you're asking such imprecise questions. I prefer these questions of (inaudible). I can't believe that your questions are so imprecise and they're not logical. I apologise, but that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you're not to say anything about the quality of questions. Counsel is a very experienced counsel and she knows what she's asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am in an embarrassing situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can say it's imprecise, but be please more careful. But please don't comment on the quality of the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In any conversation you had with Mr. Delalic, prior to your interview in Celebici, did you ask him to talk to the doctors on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you were told by Pavo that the reason the doctors had been imprisoned was because they had treated wounded Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that you look at your statement again, the statement that you gave to the office of the Prosecutor. And I am referring to page 3 in English and there is a paragraph that begins, when you're talking about when you first got to Celebici, "The camp manager, a balding man, came out and introduced himself as Pavo." Can you find that paragraph for me, please, in the Bosnian version. I'm sorry, that's actually the wrong paragraph. Let me just find -- let me move on, sir, while I find that later on. Now, sir, the prisoners that you interviewed, they knew you were with Bosnian State Television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Yes, because we introduced ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time, did you believe that even if the prisoners were being mistreated, they would be in a position to tell a reporter from Bosnian State Television about it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: They talked completely freely. And even the doctor, he wanted to add something and we aired that. We wanted to do that and aired it because we knew that also the doctors initially were there as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And had the prisoners, if the prisoners had told you that they were being mistreated, would you have broadcast that? Or let me ask it a different way. Did you tell the prisoners that if they told you that they'd been mistreated, you would not broadcast it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I didn't tell them that, but I'll answer your first question. Namely, I would send that by link to the Bosnian and Herzegovina television. I don't know whether they would air it, but I would send it. I am a reporter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that, at that time, if the prisoners -- they could have suffered some adverse consequences, had a negative report been publicised while they were still in prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the question directly? They would have been punished if they would have spoken the truth. Ask the question directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I actually think it's a matter of common sense, so let me just move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He does not have the same level of common sense as you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, it depends on what you regard as truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did it occur to you that at the time you were interviewing them, that if it was publicised that the prisoners were being mistreated, that it would have negative consequences for them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I didn't consider that. They were alone. It was up to them to tell me. You could see in the film that nobody was standing nearby while the prisoners were talking to us. Once more, Jadranka Milosevic was asking the questions on the basis of the previous answers and linking them up. He said they were wounded and then she asked, wounded by what? That's logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would also agree with me, sir, that it's logical that even if no one was there when the prisoners were answering you, the prisoners would have known that their answers would have been published, would be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just going to object to that. That's speculative. You're asking this witness to guess as to what the prisoners would think or say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a question for argument, rather than of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me that even then you realised that the prisoner who was in charge of the distribution of food would be likely to be well fed and, in fact, you made a joke about it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I didn't have the time to consider these aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse me for one minute. Sir, I am going to direct your attention to your prior statement and I am referring to page 4, at least of the English, a paragraph that begins, "Subsequently, Jadranka was interested to talk to the man who was in charge of distribution of food." And your statement then says, "He was well fed, so I joked that one can see that he was in charge of food."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question -- well, he already said that he did not do this. So my question is, does he remember saying that in your statement to the office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, I understood you to say that you did not consider then that the prisoner who was in charge of food would be likely to be well fed and you did not make a joke about it. And so I am asking you whether or not you now remember saying that to the office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: After the -- we had a relaxed conversation with Madam Sabine. We talked for two days. And the result of that conversation was this: I believe I remember that I said that I joked about it because the man looked pretty well. That was the atmosphere, I could make a joke. They didn't tell us that there were any strict rules about our behaviour. It was informal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, the video that you were shown yesterday showing your interview in Celebici, was that the entire uncut version of your visit to Celebici or are there parts that were not shown yesterday here?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: You'll have to first shoot the material, but then, because for reasons of continuity, you have to edit it then. You have first, then, entire raw footage and we had, I don't know how many minutes, and then you have to reduce it to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I did not ask you about your process of editing. My question is just, I understand that there was an edited version and there is an unedited version. My question is, is what we saw in court yesterday, is that the entire unedited version of your visit to Celebici or are there other parts of it that were not shown yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: That was raw footage. It was broadcast on the air, a shorter version, where some scenes were left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was what -- the raw footage we saw yesterday, was that the entire raw footage? Everything that there is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought he had just said some scenes are left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He said some scenes were left out from the broadcast version on television, which I understand. And I also understand that what we saw yesterday was raw footage. My question is, are there other parts of raw footage that exist that we did not see yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I take it then --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: I apologise. We had also the filming of the Delalic statement, which was subsequently shot and which was added to it. After Celebici, it was shot after Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that there were parts of your visit to Celebici, including parts of the conversations you had with the detainees, that were not recorded?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, I am just clarifying or just -- that you did not videotape the whole time you were there at Celebici and you did not videotape all of your conversations with the detainees? I am not criticising you for it, I am just clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic, Continued:
utterances.text: Well, who would do that all the time? Can you imagine the batteries, the tapes, the improvisations, the entering, the exit?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
